sources.title: Great Court architecture
take: Use a central space only when it distributes visitors and reveals multiple onward destinations.
Let vistas change as the visitor moves instead of presenting one static symmetrical postcard.
avoid: Do not copy the glass-roof aesthetic or circular Reading Room literally.
Do not spend area on an empty monumental lobby with no circulation job.
sources.why: A central reveal is valuable only when it improves orientation, route choice and spatial depth.

sources.title: Shining new light on sculpture — Cour Marly and Cour Puget
take: Use level changes and controlled overhead light to create hierarchy and varied vistas.
Treat daylight as something to regulate rather than as a permanent theatrical beam.
avoid: Do not use monumental sculpture as filler for literary space.
Do not equate a glass roof with museum quality.
sources.why: Large-scale museum drama can coexist with controlled light and clear hierarchy without dictating Hall form.

sources.title: Michael C. Rockefeller Wing reopening
take: Combine a strong trajectory and long anchor sightlines with smaller focus galleries for close looking.
Let collection needs shape display zones without turning them into themed scenery.
avoid: Do not repeat equal bays with equal visual weight.
Do not copy regional motifs unrelated to Russian literary material.
sources.why: Hall needs an establishing route and intimate poet-scale moments rather than one uniform corridor.

sources.title: Floor plans
take: Use chronology as a possible navigation simplifier without fixing a wing count in advance.
Make it possible to focus on one historical period without traversing the whole collection.
avoid: Do not turn chronological grouping into four preordained wings.
Do not require a complete linear traversal to reach a later period.
sources.why: Chronology is useful when it lowers navigation cost, not when it becomes architectural dogma.

sources.title: Walls of the new National Portrait Gallery
take: Choose wall material, reflectance and colour to improve how the actual portrait reads under controlled light.
Test portrait, background surface and lighting together instead of treating the wall as decoration.
avoid: Do not assign a loud unique colour world or material archetype to every poet.
Do not default to black metallic walls and glowing gold frames.
sources.why: The portrait is the optical anchor; the background should support it rather than advertise a theme.

sources.title: Museum Lighting Research
take: Treat lighting for paper and documentary objects as a conservation constraint as well as visual design.
Separate circulation lighting decisions from fragile-object display lighting.
avoid: Do not use one dramatic lighting recipe for portraits, photographs, paper and architecture.
Do not rescue weak display composition with brighter spotlights.
sources.why: Light-sensitive documents need a different exposure strategy from the readable circulation environment.

sources.title: Smithsonian Guidelines for Accessible Exhibition Design
take: Design a clearly legible circulation route with adequate clear widths, viewing clearances and headroom.
Avoid glare, abrupt light transitions and obstacles that make the route hard to read.
avoid: Do not treat accessibility as a post-build UI overlay.
Do not rely on narrow one-person routes where visitors must stop to view exhibits.
sources.why: Accessible dimensions and visual legibility are geometry inputs for the greybox, not late compliance patches.

sources.title: Accessibility at the museum
take: Provide direct accessible routes, rest opportunities and multiple information modalities.
Preserve equivalent content outside any future 3D interaction.
avoid: Do not make free locomotion a prerequisite for reaching content.
Do not make Canvas the sole owner of navigation or interpretation.
sources.why: The spatial experience can be optional; the content and route logic must remain accessible independently.

sources.title: Caring for paper objects
take: Treat light exposure to sensitive paper as cumulative and keep display illumination low and controlled.
Use rotation, exposure limits or facsimile strategies when appropriate.
avoid: Do not expose manuscripts to the same bright route lighting as architecture.
Do not infer reproduction rights from conservation guidance.
sources.why: A credible literary museum needs controlled document pockets and rights/provenance decisions separate from visual mood.

sources.institution: All-Russian Museum of A. S. Pushkin
sources.title: Pushkin. Life and Work
take: Use one strong portrait as a visual anchor and let smaller documentary material form the surrounding evidence field.
Keep the first Pushkin slice object-led rather than filling it with equivalent decorative niches.
avoid: Do not assume the museum webpage grants image reproduction rights.
Do not copy the physical room literally without a Hall-specific spatial test.
sources.why: Pushkin provides a concrete exhibit hierarchy to test while object-level image rights remain a separate gate.

sensitivePaperGuidance.note: Use roughly 50 lux or as low as practical as an evidence guide; final exposure strategy is object-specific and remains a conservation/rights decision.

spatialHypotheses.name: orientation court plus chronological branches
spatialHypotheses.question: Can a central orientation/reveal space distribute visitors into chronological groups without becoming an empty monumental lobby?
mustTest: At least one onward destination is visibly legible from orientation.
Branch identity works without giant floating labels.
Return path avoids long dead travel.
Central space has a visual and circulation reason to exist with UI hidden.
spatialHypotheses.primaryFailureMode: Impressive centre followed by repetitive peripheral corridors.

spatialHypotheses.name: directed chronological promenade plus focus bays
spatialHypotheses.question: Can a primarily linear route communicate literary chronology without recreating Hall v2's uniform nave?
mustTest: Compression, release and sightline vary deliberately along the route.
Poet focus bays do not block the main trajectory.
A visitor can jump to a later period without traversing every prior poet.
No sequence of equivalent wall niches defines the experience.

spatialHypotheses.name: asymmetric orientation plus diagonal or curved trajectory and side focus rooms
spatialHypotheses.question: Can a less symmetrical museum create stronger cinematic sightlines and anchor works while retaining clear wayfinding?
mustTest: Entry has one clear establishing direction.
The long view terminates on a meaningful exhibit or architectural anchor.
Side rooms support close reading and a clear return to orientation.
Portrait-mobile framing remains viable without geometry crossing the screen.
spatialHypotheses.primaryFailureMode: Visually exciting but confusing spatial graph.

automaticRejectionRules: Strongest view depends on ornament, dome, bloom, fog, particles or lighting effects absent in neutral grey.
Intended route exposes unfinished backs or sides of architecture.
First poet reads like a card attached to a wall instead of an exhibit composition.
Equivalent bays repeat without spatial hierarchy.
Route requires FPS or free-look to become understandable.
Large HUD labels are required for basic wayfinding.
Portrait-mobile crop has no viable framing without rebuilding geometry.
Central or transition space exists only for spectacle.
Candidate survives only because more time has already been spent on it.
